posts.name: Dougie Kass
posts.text:
I have written 267 columns ("More Tales From Nvidia") on The StreetPro over the last two years. @TheStreetPro 

I have expressed a number of concerns (from a lay person's perspective) - some of which Roger McNamee and I share in common:

*  Society is ill prepared for the negative consequences and safety issues associated with AI.

*  The AI creators and practitioners take no responsibility for those consequences and issues.  Indeed, they are trying to the opposite - evading accountability.

* The reality of AI has fallen far short of expectations and applications.

*  Thus far the apparent absence of enterprise customers (who pay more for AI services than it costs a vendor to provide them), the benefits of scaling training sets and data centers and the widely anticipated productivity gains have been slow to materialize.

* The limitations of large language models is growing more apparent. The systems are inherently probabilistic - resulting in varying degrees of errors and non-predictive results. Those shortcomings are not being overcome by scaling computer power.

* A one size fits all product requires massive amounts of time and money to integrate into existing systems - with limitations already developing on funding.

* The speed to market and scale of AI investment failed to wait for innovation to drive down the price of infrastructure (in fact the opposite is happening with costs rising)  and has created not only a timing problem between outlays and revenues but (also) potential risk to the bond and the broader economy far worse than the Internet era.

* Though more than two handfuls of companies are in competition with different AI products, history shows that only a few will likely be successful. The potential for hundreds of billions of dollars of writeoffs is rising.

* The size of AI infrastructure investment and the amount of debt being employed is inflationary, raises interest rates and crowds out other borrowers. Already investors' appetite appears to becoming sated and companies like $CRWV CoreWeave (a short) and $ORCL Oracle (also a short) are already "in distress" with extended balance sheets and off shore financing.

* Other risks from AI products include fraud, cybersecurity, deskilling workers and students and social isolation.

* AI concentrates power in the hands of a few - some of whom have previously expressed authoritarian tendencies.

From Roger McNamee:

Roger McNamee: AI’s ‘existential risks’ are all hype. But there's a real, and dangerous, financial bubble building 
https://www.thenerve.news/p/roger-mcnamee-ai-risks-financial-stability-deskilling-errors-bubble-burst

posts.name: Robin Brooks
posts.text: Yes. In EM you would have just had a currency devaluation. The Euro zone has delayed that devaluation with these TARGET2 flows. Easiest way to see this is to think what would happen if TARGET2 goes to zero. It would require the ECB to sell all its sovereign debt holdings. Yields would spike and we’d be in a big crisis.

posts.name: Robin Brooks
posts.text: The problem is that German politicians and their proxies at the ECB know all this very well, but everyone has an incentive to kick the can a little further down the road so that the eventual and inevitable blow-up doesn’t happen on their watch. What’s needed are claw-backs so these people act responsibly and don’t scurry off before the blow-up.

posts.name: Robin Brooks
posts.text: No. Germany’s TARGET2 claims are basically the counterpart to artificial yield caps and big currency overvaluations on the high-debt periphery. There is no netting this out. Without these claims, periphery currencies would have devalued massively and of course they still might one day…

posts.name: Robin Brooks
posts.text: No. Easiest way is to draw the contrast with any EM debt crisis. Private capital flows collapse and the currency devalues. That’s not possible in the Euro, so private flows got replaced by official ones, ie ECB purchases of public debt under QE. That artificially caps yields and props up currencies that are really much weaker.

posts.name: Capital Edge Notes
posts.text:
Brent +10% maps to gold −4% and silver −8%, on Brooks's numbers from the second half of October.
I think this is a hot-war liquidity trade, not a rates trade.
US real 10y yields fell about 30bp in October while Brent rose 13.6%, and that should have helped gold.
Two weeks of daily data is a short window, so I'd treat the link as fragile if Hormuz reopens.

quoted.text:
